Modular operator superposition (MOS): A physics-guided machine learning framework for addressing the curse of dimensionality and multiscale challenges in computational fluid dynamics
Article preview
Abstract
Keywords
abstract: AbstractWe introduce Modular Operator Superposition (MOS), a physics-guided and AI-augmented framework for efficient, scalable, and generalizable flow field modeling in high-dimensional and multiscale fluid systems. Rather than globally resolving flow fields via mesh-based discretization, MOS decomposes the system into physically meaningful flow primitives, each represented by a reusable modular operator. These operators are trained offline using a parameterized physics-informed neural network (P-PINN) in a single pre-processing step, and later composed through a physics-guided superposition strategy to approximate the full system-level mapping. The core advantage of MOS lies in its modularization strategy. By learning only small-scale flow primitives offline, MOS reduces the training cost to a fixed, minimal investment independent of system-level complexity. In the online stage, MOS dynamically solves for primitive-level interactions for any specific configuration of a system, then reconstructs the global flow field through the superposition of modular outputs. This two-stage online process, comprising both solving and inference, enables scalable and generalizable predictions. As a result, MOS addresses the curse of dimensionality by reducing high-dimensional systems to tractable compositions of modular operators and overcomes multiscale challenges through a scale-adaptive operator assembly that flexibly resolves flow features with minimal overhead. We demonstrate MOS for static and dynamic arrays of up to 15,000 cylinders in a channel cross-flow (corresponding to roughly 105 input parameters). All of these configurations are solved using a shared single-cylinder cross-flow modular operator, trained offline in 30 hours using a data-free, physics-informed machine learning strategy. In the online stage, MOS achieves end-to-end flow field prediction at 3 to 5 orders of magnitude speedup over conventional numerical solvers, while maintaining high fidelity (𝑅2>0.85 for all cases). Moreover, the MOS solution format requires 3 to 5 orders of magnitude lower memory usage than conventional numerical outputs. Once solved, the solution can be queried in real-time to infer flow variables at arbitrary spatial resolutions or scattered points, enabling flexible and efficient visualization across scales. Additional tests indicate that MOS remains robust to polydispersity and translational/rotational motion of the cylinders.

  - heading "Introduction" [level=2]
  - generic: "In recent years, machine learning (ML) has been rapidly advancing computational fluid dynamics (CFD) by improving efficiency, accuracy, scalability, and adaptability [43], [57], [99], [100], [101]. Leveraging its fast inference and universal function approximation capabilities, ML has been augmenting CFD in multiple ways: (i) Surrogate modeling: ML-driven surrogate models accelerate flow field evaluations by orders of magnitude, replacing iterative numerical solvers with direct inference. Deep neural networks [43], [46], [47], [48], [83], [89], [90], [93], [95], [102], [103] and operator-learning methods [16], [44], [49], [53], [54], [55], [60] enable accurate and fast predictions. Hybrid ML-augmented solvers [9], [14], [18], [38], [72], [77], [84], [85], [97], [106] further improve computational efficiency of numerical simulations. (ii) Physical model enhancement: ML has extended CFD’s applicability in large-scale, multiphysics problems. Data-driven models for turbulence [10], [22], [23], [56], [65], [66], [75], [82], [91], [92], [96], multiphase flows [20], [31], [33], [37], [61], [62], [70], [71], [78], [87], [88], combustion [30], [36], and synthetic boundary conditions [5], [28], [67], [86], [104] have improved sub-grid closure fidelity. Additionally, super-resolution methods push beyond grid-based limitations [21], [26], [29], [74], [76]. (iii) Physics-informed learning: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and neural operators integrate physical laws into ML frameworks [24], [40], [42], [80], [81]. These approaches alleviate dependence on labeled data, providing greater flexibility in under-resolved or data-scarce regimes. (iv) High-dimensional parameterization: Unlike traditional CFD solvers that require case-by-case simulations, parameterized ML models can infer flow solutions across broad parametric spaces. This enables efficient evaluation over varying geometries, boundary conditions, and material properties, making them particularly valuable in design optimization and real-time control tasks [11], [12], [16], [17], [32], [39], [41], [44], [50], [51], [52], [53], [54], [55], [58], [59], [60]. Together, these advancements demonstrate the growing role of ML in modern CFD workflows, particularly in accelerating flow prediction, improving physical modeling, enabling scalable optimization, and supporting real-time control applications."
  - generic: "Despite these advancements, several long-standing and fundamental challenges continue to limit the practical implementation of ML in CFD applications [1], [15], [73], [98], [105]: (i) Generalization and extrapolation limitations: Irrespective of data-driven or physics-informed, ML methods are high-dimensional interpolation algorithms [63] and therefore struggle to generalize beyond regimes explicitly “seen” during training. The distinction between interpolation and extrapolation can be subtle in fluid dynamics due to flow universalities (e.g., symmetry, self-similarity, scaling laws) [13], [27]. Here we use “extrapolation” to broadly refer to generalization to untrained configurations in geometry, complexity, and scale. Small changes in input parameters (e.g., geometry, boundary conditions, or flow regime) outside the original training scope often require retraining or fine-tuning, restricting practical adaptability. (ii) Prohibitive training costs: Real-world CFD applications often involve high-dimensional input parameter spaces and wide-ranging flow scales, particularly in turbulence, multiphase flows, and reactive flows. For data-driven methods, the cost of generating high-fidelity datasets that sufficiently cover this space is computationally infeasible due to the curse of dimensionality. Physics-informed methods, while not explicitly reliant on training data (i.e., physics-informed still require collocation points in the parameter space to enforce the PDE-driven loss), can suffer from fast-growing training cost and convergence difficulty as problem size increases [45], limiting their effectiveness in large-scale or multiscale problems. (iii) Offline-online trade-off: ML-based surrogate models typically rely on heavy offline training to achieve robust online performance. However, as aforementioned, both data-driven and physics-informed training processes are constrained by cost and generalization limits. Meanwhile, ML-augmented solvers (e.g., subgrid closures or embedded neural components) avoid offline training but remain closely tied to conventional discretization frameworks and are less suited to efficient parameterized evaluations across diverse configurations."
  - generic: "At the time, a unified ML-CFD framework that simultaneously achieves both efficiency and generalizability remains elusive. At the core of this challenge lie two fundamental issues: the high dimensionality of the input space and the multiscale complexity of the output field. Input high-dimensionality originates from the large number of independent parameters required to characterize real fluid systems, including geometric configurations, boundary conditions, and physical properties. In conventional CFD, this leads to an explosion in the number of required simulations, making the approach computationally prohibitive. In ML-based methods, this same input complexity demands that the trained model effectively generalize across a vast parameter space, which is often an unrealistic expectation without excessive data or model capacity. On the other hand, the output complexity arises from the inherent multiscale nature of fluid dynamics, where physical quantities vary over several orders of magnitude in space and time. This imposes strict grid resolution requirements, increases the burden of solution representation, and poses challenges for model approximation and training. Together, these two challenges form a fundamental bottleneck: many high-dimensional, multiscale engineering problems remain intractable under current CFD frameworks and are only partially alleviated even with state-of-the-art ML methods."
  - generic: "Inspired by recent advancements in ML and multiphase flow studies [2], [3], [4], [7], [68], we propose a new ML-CFD hybrid methodology, Modular Operator Superposition (MOS), specifically tailored to address the fundamental challenges of high-dimensionality and multiscale complexity. In MOS, each primitive flow operator captures a localized feature (e.g., wake formation), and complex flows are reconstructed as a hierarchical superposition of these primitives across macro, meso, and micro scales. A physics-guided coupling scheme governs both mutual interactions and cross-scale feedback, enabling MOS to flexibly assemble reusable modules into new configurations. By decoupling the global problem into composable building blocks, MOS delivers scalable, generalizable flow solutions with a dramatically reduced offline training burden. At the core of MOS is a parameterized physics-informed neural network (P-PINN) that learns each primitive operator over a continuous parameter space [58], [59]. Training on local primitives instead of full-domain simulations makes the learning process computationally tractable and inherently robust. Once trained, these parameterized modules plug into “unseen” flow scenarios without retraining or fine-tuning. To bridge scales, MOS applies an explicit divide-and-conquer superposition: fine-scale dynamics are resolved by the P-PINN, then seamlessly embedded into larger-scale contexts via a physics-consistent projection. Conceptually akin to building with adaptive LEGO bricks, each brick “morphs” to its surroundings, this unified framework promises to overcome the traditional trade-off between efficiency and generalization in CFD. While the MOS framework is compatible with data-driven strategies, the implementation in this study is purely physics-driven: all modular operators are trained using P-PINN without any reliance on precomputed data, thereby eliminating the offline cost of dataset preparation."
  - generic: The applicability of MOS is inherently tied to a specific class of multiscale flows, namely, those in which the separation of scales is clearly delineated by distinguishable physical markers. These markers allow the flow domain to be decomposed into small-scale primitives with commonalities that serve as the basis for modular operator learning. In this study, we illustrate the MOS framework using the example of incompressible flow through a two-dimensional channel populated with randomly distributed rigid cylinders. Here, the locations and configurations of the cylinders act as physical markers, each inducing a similar local perturbation to the global flow and enabling modular representation. The same principle naturally extends to three-dimensional multiphase flows involving a dispersed phase, such as spherical particles suspended in a carrier fluid, where each particle defines a localized region of small-scale interaction (e.g., wake structures). Similar opportunities arise in environmental and geophysical flows, such as canopy flows over submerged aquatic vegetation, wastewater clarification using deflector baffles, air-sand interactions over dune fields, and urban air pollution modeling. In all these cases, the presence of identifiable localized primitives with repeated or similar influence on the flow field provides a physically meaningful basis for applying the MOS methodology.
  - generic: "The objectives of this study are threefold: (i) To formally establish the Modular Operator Superposition (MOS) framework by articulating its theoretical foundation and computational workflow. (ii) To demonstrate its effectiveness through application to a representative problem (i.e., a two-dimensional channel cross-flow over a randomly distributed cylinder array). (iii) To comprehensively evaluate its capabilities by examining its performance characteristics, practical limitations, and potential directions for future research."
